lines.text: Gus dug a pool so deep that a beach ball shrinks to a basketball at the bottom.
It's Saturday morning, and Gus wants the deepest pool on his street: a hundred feet, straight down.
The dirt fills almost two hundred dump trucks, and the garden hose runs for over three weeks.
His neighbor laughs. Deep water, he says, is just more water.
So Gus tests it with a beach ball. It won't go under: full of air, it pushes up with sixty pounds.
He ties it to a hundred-pound barbell and lowers it on a rope.
At thirty-four feet, the ball is half its size. At a hundred, a quarter: a wrinkled thing no bigger than a basketball.
But wait. Nobody is touching it. So what makes it shrink?
You see, water is heavy. Think of the bottom pancake in a tall stack: it carries all the others, so it gets squashed.
Down there, the ball is the bottom pancake.
Thirty-four feet of water weigh as much as all the air above your head, right up to space.
So at a hundred feet, the ball carries four skies.
And every floor tile, one foot wide, holds up three tons of water.
Luckily, squeezed air isn't lost. Gus pulls the rope, and the ball grows right back.
So of his hundred feet of pool, he uses the top two.
